extraction_notes.note: The one-sentence proof idea of Proposition 1 is a proof sketch, which the prompt says gets rigor semi_formal, but rigor is not allowed on proof nodes (finalize warns); rigor was omitted and the proves edge marked alternative.

The sentence stating the cited reverse-time SDE also defines the (conditional) score function in its 'where' clause; the sentence cannot be split, so the score function has no definition node of its own.

TP2 is a one-sentence attribution of strong existence/uniqueness to Assumption 1(a) (theorem vs remark); ClP5 asserts the explicit Gaussian transition of the forward OU process without proof (claim vs equation-bearing definition).
The notation for forward/reverse/simulated densities used in the proof of Lemma 1 is given only in a table; the introducing sentence and the table are kept as one definition node.

Running-text derivations in Appendix C.2 that establish (60)-(61) and monotonicity of the posterior covariance trace, used by later proofs; emitted as claims rather than remarks because they are cited as results.

Numerical tables, the itemized interpretation of the error terms after Proposition 2, the literature comparison paragraphs, experiment hyperparameter tables and the future-research directions of the conclusion were not extracted; only summary empirical findings are kept as numerical claims.

nodes.name: Identity matrix $I_d$
nodes.statement: The identity matrix in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is denoted by $I_d$, where $d$ is the dimension.

nodes.name: Multivariate Gaussian distribution and density
nodes.statement: We use $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ to denote the multivariate Gaussian distribution with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, and $\mathcal{N}(\cdot; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ the corresponding Gaussian density function.

nodes.name: L2/spectral norm and Frobenius norm
nodes.statement: We denote by $\|\cdot\|$ the $L_2$ norm/spectral norm of vectors/matrices, and by $\|\cdot\|_F$ the Frobenius norm of matrices.

nodes.name: L-Lipschitz function
nodes.statement: A function $f$ is called $L$-Lipschitz, where $L>0$, if $||f( \mathbf{x}) - f( \mathbf{x}')||_2 \le L||\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'||_2$ for any $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}'$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic inequality notation $\lesssim$
nodes.statement: We employ the notation $x \lesssim y$ to indicate that $x \leq Cy$ for some positive constant $C > 0$, and define $x \gtrsim y$ analogously.

nodes.name: Order equivalence notation $\asymp$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we write $x \asymp y$ if there exist constants $C_1, C_2 > 0$ such that $C_1y \leq x \leq C_2y$.

nodes.name: Distribution of a random variable
nodes.statement: For a random variable $\mathbf{X}$, its distribution is denoted by $P_{\mathbf{X}}$.

nodes.name: Equality in distribution and absolute continuity
nodes.statement: We write $\mathbf{X} \overset{d}{=} \mathbf{Y}$ if $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ have the same distribution, and $P_{\mathbf{X}} \ll P_{\mathbf{Y}}$ if $P_{\mathbf{X}}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to (w.r.t.) $P_{\mathbf{Y}}$.

nodes.name: Mutually absolutely continuous (equivalent) distributions
nodes.statement: Two distributions $P_{\mathbf{X}}$ and $P_{\mathbf{Y}}$ are said to be mutually absolutely continuous, or equivalent, if $P_{\mathbf{X}} \ll P_{\mathbf{Y}}$ and $P_{\mathbf{Y}} \ll P_{\mathbf{X}}$.

nodes.name: Kullback-Leibler divergence
nodes.statement_short: KL divergence as the integral of the log Radon-Nikodym derivative, $+\infty$ without absolute continuity.
nodes.statement: The Kullback--Leibler (KL) between probability distributions $P_{\mathbf{X}}$ and $P_{\mathbf{Y}}$ is $ \text{KL}(P_{\mathbf{X}} || P_{\mathbf{Y}}) := \int \log(\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\mathbf{X}}}{\mathrm{d} P_{\mathbf{Y}}}) \mathrm{d} P_{\mathbf{X}}$ if $P_{\mathbf{X}} \ll P_{\mathbf{Y}}$, and is defined to be $+\infty$ otherwise.

nodes.name: Target SDE
nodes.statement_short: The unknown $d$-dimensional SDE $dX=\mu dt+\sigma dW$ whose paths are to be generated.
nodes.statement: Consider a $d$-dimensional \textit{target} SDE defined on a filtered probability space $\big(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}, \{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{0\le t\le T}\big)$:\begin{equation} \mathrm{d}\mathbf{X}(t) = \mu(t, \mathbf{X}(t))\mathrm{d} t + \sigma(t, \mathbf{X}(t))\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}(t),\ t \in [0, T], \end{equation} where $\mu: [0, T] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ is the drift coefficient, $\sigma: [0, T] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{d\times m}$ is the diffusion coefficient, and $\mathbf{W}$ is a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion.

nodes.name: Eq. (1): target SDE
nodes.statement: \mathrm{d}\mathbf{X}(t) = \mu(t, \mathbf{X}(t))\mathrm{d} t + \sigma(t, \mathbf{X}(t))\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}(t),\ t \in [0, T],
nodes.label: eq: target_SDE

nodes.name: Fixed initial state and unique strong solution
nodes.statement: We assume that the equation starts from a fixed, known initial state $\mathbf{X}(0)\equiv \mathbf{x}(0)\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and has a unique strong solution.

nodes.name: SDE path generation problem
nodes.statement_short: Given only i.i.d. sample paths of an SDE with unknown coefficients, generate new paths with the same distribution.
nodes.statement: However, both functions $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are \textit{unknown,} and we have access only to a set of i.i.d. sample paths of the SDE \eqref{eq: target_SDE} on $[0, T]$. Our goal, in mathematical terms, is to generate additional sample paths that exhibit the same distributional properties as those of the {\it unknown} SDE \eqref{eq: target_SDE}.

nodes.name: Uniform time grid $\mathcal{T}$
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we consider a uniform grid $\mathcal{T} := \{t_n: t_n = n\Delta t\ \text{for}\ n=0, 1, ..., N_T\}$ with a fixed time step $\Delta t > 0$ and assume that the number of discrete epochs $N_T = T / \Delta t$ is an integer.

nodes.name: Observed dataset of sample paths
nodes.statement: The dataset available to us, therefore, consists of $H > 1$ sample paths of $\{\mathbf{X}(t): t \in [0, T]\}$ observed at grid points in $\mathcal{T}$ (i.e. time series), denoted by \begin{align} \left\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_0), \mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_1), \cdots, \mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_{N_T}),\quad i=1, ..., H\right\}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Eq. (2): obs data
nodes.statement: \left\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_0), \mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_1), \cdots, \mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_{N_T}),\quad i=1, ..., H\right\}.
nodes.label: eq: obs_data

nodes.name: Conditioning variable $\mathbf{C}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{C}$ be an unknown random variable (e.g., a covariate).

nodes.name: Conditional target distribution
nodes.statement: Conditional diffusion models aim to generate new samples from an unknown (conditional) target distribution $p_{\text{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}):= q_0(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) $ on $\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{target}}}$ given $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c}$, when one has access to a set of independent training data $\{(\mathbf{c}_i, \mathbf{y}_i(0)): \mathbf{c}_i\sim\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{y}_i(0)\sim q_0(\cdot | \mathbf{c}_i), i=1,\cdots N\}$.

nodes.name: Forward OU noising process
nodes.statement_short: Noise the conditional target with a time-inhomogeneous OU process run up to horizon $T_g$.
nodes.statement: To achieve this, the conditional diffusion model first noises the target distribution with a (non-homogeneous) Ornstein--Uhlenbeck (OU) process: \begin{align} \mathrm{d}\mathbf{Y}(\tau) = -f(\tau)\mathbf{Y}(\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau + g(\tau) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}(\tau),\ \mathbf{Y}(0)\sim q_0(\cdot | \mathbf{c}),\ \tau\in [0, T_g], \end{align} where $\mathbf{B}$ is a standard Brownian motion in $\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{target}}}$ that is independent of $\mathbf{Y}(0)$, and $T_g$ is a fixed horizon length (e.g. $T_g =1$).

nodes.name: Eq. (3): forward SDE DDPM
nodes.statement: \mathrm{d}\mathbf{Y}(\tau) = -f(\tau)\mathbf{Y}(\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau + g(\tau) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}(\tau),\ \mathbf{Y}(0)\sim q_0(\cdot | \mathbf{c}),\ \tau\in [0, T_g],
nodes.label: eq: forward_SDE_DDPM

nodes.name: Linear noise schedule $\beta(\tau)=a\tau+b$
nodes.origin_citation: Ho et al. 2020; Song et al.
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper, we consider the popular choice of $f(\tau): = \frac{1}{2}\beta(\tau),\ g(\tau): = \sqrt{\beta(\tau)},\ \beta(\tau) := a\tau + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are pre-specified positive constants \citep{ho2020denoising, songscore}.

nodes.name: Forward process and its analytical solution
nodes.statement: The noising process \eqref{eq: forward_SDE_DDPM} is called the \textit{forward process} which admits an analytical solution \begin{align*} \mathbf{Y}(\tau) &= e^{-\int_0^\tau f(v)\mathrm{d} v}\mathbf{Y}(0) + \int_{0}^\tau e^{-\int_u^\tau f(v)\mathrm{d} v}g(u) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{B}(u). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Marginal density $q_\tau(\cdot|\mathbf{c})$
nodes.statement: Given a condition $\mathbf{c}$, we let the marginal density of $\mathbf{Y}(\tau)$ be $q_\tau(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$, which is unknown due to the unknown $p_{\text{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$.

nodes.name: Conditional Gaussian transition $q_{\tau|0}$
nodes.statement: When $\mathbf{Y}(0) = \mathbf{y}(0)$ is given, the conditional distribution of $\mathbf{Y}(\tau)$ is clearly Gaussian and known, which we denote by $q_{\tau|0}(\cdot |\mathbf{y}(0), \mathbf{c})$.

nodes.name: Reverse denoising process
nodes.statement: Consider the reverse (in time) denoising process $\{\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}(\tau):= \mathbf{Y}(T_g - \tau), \tau\in[0, T_g]\}$.

nodes.name: Reverse-time SDE (Anderson)
assumptions: Under mild assumptions
conclusions: $\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}$ satisfies the reverse SDE starting from $\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}(0)\sim q_{T_g}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$
nodes.statement_short: The time-reversed forward process solves a reverse SDE whose drift involves the conditional score $\nabla\log q_\tau$.
nodes.origin_citation: Anderson 1982; Cattiaux et al. 2023; Haussmann & Pardoux 1986
nodes.statement: Under mild assumptions \citep{Anderson1982, cattiaux2023time, haussmann1986time}, $\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}$ satisfies the reverse SDE starting from $\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}(0)\sim q_{T_g}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$: \begin{align} \mathrm{d}\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}(\tau) = [f(T_g - \tau)\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}(\tau) + g^2(T_g - \tau) \nabla\log q_{T_g - \tau}(\tilde {\mathbf{Y}}(\tau) | \mathbf{c})]\mathrm{d}\tau + g(T_g - \tau) \mathrm{d}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}(\tau), \end{align} where $\nabla\log q_{\tau}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$ is called the (conditional) score function and is unknown.

nodes.name: Eq. (4): reverse SDE DDPM
nodes.statement: \mathrm{d}\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}(\tau) = [f(T_g - \tau)\tilde{\mathbf{Y}}(\tau) + g^2(T_g - \tau) \nabla\log q_{T_g - \tau}(\tilde {\mathbf{Y}}(\tau) | \mathbf{c})]\mathrm{d}\tau + g(T_g - \tau) \mathrm{d}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}(\tau),
nodes.label: eq: reverse_SDE_DDPM

nodes.name: Explicit score matching
nodes.statement_short: Train a network $s_\theta$ to minimize the time-integrated $L^2$ error to the true conditional score.
nodes.statement: To learn the unknown conditional score, one can consider training a neural network $s_\theta$ parameterized by $\theta$ to minimize $\int_{0}^{T_g}\mathbb{E}\|s_\theta(\tau, \mathbf{Y}(\tau), \mathbf{c}) - \nabla\log q_\tau(\mathbf{Y}(\tau) | \mathbf{c})\|^2\mathrm{d} \tau$.

nodes.name: Denoising score matching
nodes.statement_short: Weighted regression of $s_\theta$ onto the known Gaussian transition score $\nabla\log q_{\tau|0}$.
nodes.statement: In this paper, we apply the following denoising score matching procedure \citep{songscore, vincent2011connection}: \begin{align} \min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim \text{Unif}[0, T_g]} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(0)} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(\tau)|(\mathbf{Y}(0), \mathbf{c})}\bigg[\lambda(\tau)\big\| s_\theta(\tau, \mathbf{Y}(\tau), \mathbf{c}) - \nabla\log q_{\tau|0}(\mathbf{Y}(\tau) | \mathbf{Y}(0), \mathbf{c})\big\|^2\bigg], \end{align} where $\text{Unif}[0, T_g]$ is the uniform distribution on $[0, T_g]$, $\mathbf{Y}(0)\sim p_{\text{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$, $\mathbf{Y}(\tau) | (\mathbf{Y}(0), \mathbf{c}) \sim q_{\tau|0}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$ which is Gaussian, and $\lambda: [0, T_g]\to \mathbb{R}_{+}$ is some positive weighting function.

nodes.name: Eq. (5): denosing score matching
nodes.statement: \min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim \text{Unif}[0, T_g]} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(0)} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(\tau)|(\mathbf{Y}(0), \mathbf{c})}\bigg[\lambda(\tau)\big\| s_\theta(\tau, \mathbf{Y}(\tau), \mathbf{c}) - \nabla\log q_{\tau|0}(\mathbf{Y}(\tau) | \mathbf{Y}(0), \mathbf{c})\big\|^2\bigg],
nodes.label: eq: denosing_score_matching

nodes.name: Euler-Maruyama sampling of the conditional diffusion model
nodes.statement_short: Simulate the reverse SDE with the learned score by $K$ Euler-Maruyama steps from Gaussian noise.
nodes.statement: With the conditional score function trained and learned, the sampling process is to simulate \eqref{eq: reverse_SDE_DDPM} in $K$ steps, using the Euler--Maruyama discretization scheme with a uniform time step size of $\Delta\tau =T_g / K$. Specifically, let $\tau_k = k\Delta \tau$ and $\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(0) \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$. For $k=0,1,\cdots,K-1$, set \begin{align} \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_{k + 1}) = \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_{k}) + [\tilde f(\tau_k)\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_k) + \tilde g^2(\tau_k) s_\theta(T_g - \tau_k, \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_{k})), \mathbf{c})]\Delta\tau + \tilde g(\tau_k)\sqrt{\Delta\tau} \cdot \zeta_k, \end{align} where $\tilde f(\tau) = f(T_g - \tau), \tilde g(\tau) = g(T_g - \tau)$, and $\zeta_k$'s are i.i.d. standard Gaussian random vectors. The terminal state $\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_K)$ is a generated, desired sample.

nodes.name: Eq. (6): reverse SDE DDPM simulation
nodes.statement: \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_{k + 1}) = \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_{k}) + [\tilde f(\tau_k)\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_k) + \tilde g^2(\tau_k) s_\theta(T_g - \tau_k, \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_{k})), \mathbf{c})]\Delta\tau + \tilde g(\tau_k)\sqrt{\Delta\tau} \cdot \zeta_k,
nodes.label: eq: reverse_SDE_DDPM_simulation

nodes.name: Stochastic increment $\Delta\mathbf{X}(t;\mathbf{x})$
nodes.statement: Specifically, we generate samples of the stochastic increment $\Delta\mathbf{X}(t; \mathbf{x}) :=\mathbf{X}^{t, \mathbf{x}}(t + \Delta t) - \mathbf{x}$ defined by the solution to \eqref{eq: target_SDE} conditional on $\mathbf{X}^{t, \mathbf{x}}(t) = \mathbf{x}$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Generation of SDE Paths via Conditional Diffusion Models

nodes.name: Conditional diffusion model $G(t_n,\mathbf{x};\theta_n)$ for increments
nodes.statement_short: For each grid time, a conditional diffusion model with condition (time, state) whose output is distributed as the next increment.
nodes.statement: For each $t_n$, we set condition $\mathbf{c}_n = (t_n, \mathbf{x}(t_n))$ sampled from $\mathbf{C}_n = (t_n, \mathbf{X}(t_n))$ and train a conditional diffusion model $G(t_n, \mathbf{x}; \theta_n)$ where $\mathbf{x}(t_n)=\mathbf{x}$, such that $G(t_n, \mathbf{x}; \theta_n)$ consists of a score network $s_{\theta_n}$ trained via \eqref{eq: denosing_score_matching} and generates new samples $\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_n(\tau_K)$ distributed as $\Delta\mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x})$ by running \eqref{eq: reverse_SDE_DDPM_simulation}, i.e., \begin{align} \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_n(\tau_K)\overset{d}{\approx} \Delta \mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x}) := \mathbf{X}(t_n + \Delta t) - \mathbf{x} = \int_{t_n}^{t_n + \Delta t}\mu(t, \mathbf{X}(t))\mathrm{d} t + \int_{t_n}^{t_n + \Delta t}\sigma(t, \mathbf{X}(t))\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}(t). \end{align}
nodes.section: 2.3 Generation of SDE Paths via Conditional Diffusion Models

nodes.name: Eq. (7): objective AR gen
nodes.statement: \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_n(\tau_K)\overset{d}{\approx} \Delta \mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x}) := \mathbf{X}(t_n + \Delta t) - \mathbf{x} = \int_{t_n}^{t_n + \Delta t}\mu(t, \mathbf{X}(t))\mathrm{d} t + \int_{t_n}^{t_n + \Delta t}\sigma(t, \mathbf{X}(t))\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}(t).
nodes.section: 2.3 Generation of SDE Paths via Conditional Diffusion Models
nodes.label: eq: objective_AR_gen

nodes.name: Autoregressive path generation
nodes.statement: Next, to generate new sample paths (time series) from the unknown SDE, we start from $\hat {\mathbf{x}}(t_0) = \mathbf{x}(0)$ and recursively produce \begin{align} \hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_{n+1}) = \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_{n }) + \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_n(\tau_K),\quad \text{for}\ n = 0, ..., N_T-1. \end{align}
nodes.section: 2.3 Generation of SDE Paths via Conditional Diffusion Models

nodes.name: Eq. (8): AR generation
nodes.statement: \hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_{n+1}) = \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_{n }) + \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_n(\tau_K),\quad \text{for}\ n = 0, ..., N_T-1.
nodes.section: 2.3 Generation of SDE Paths via Conditional Diffusion Models
nodes.label: eq: AR_generation

nodes.name: Autoregressive versus whole-trajectory generation
nodes.statement_short: Generating increments autoregressively keeps the target dimension at $d$ instead of $d N_T$, allowing simple MLP score networks.
nodes.statement: Instead of using conditional diffusion models to generate SDE paths in a sequential and autoregressive fashion, an alternative approach is to train a single diffusion model to generate samples of the entire trajectory $(\mathbf{X}(t_1), \cdots, \mathbf{X}(t_{N_T}))$ directly. In such a case, the dimension of the target distribution is $d\times N_T$, which becomes large with a high-dimensional SDE (large $d$) and/or a large number of observation slots (large $N_T$). While diffusion models can indeed deal with high-dimensional distributions, they nonetheless require more complex network architectures to train the score functions and longer training times. The autoregressive approach we choose instead reduces the dimension and complexity of the generation task, which allows us to use a simple neural network such as a multilayer perceptron (MLP) for training the conditional score function, leading to a more efficient solution.
nodes.section: 2.3 Generation of SDE Paths via Conditional Diffusion Models

nodes.name: Training process of the SDE generative model
input: Training data $\{(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_n), \Delta\mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_n; \mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_n))): i=1,\cdots, H, n=0, \cdots, N_T - 1\}$
nodes.statement_short: Train one conditional score network per grid time by SGD on the denoising score matching loss over sampled increments.
nodes.statement: \small \caption{Training process of the SDE generative model $\{G(t_n, \cdot; \theta_n): n=0, \cdots, N_T - 1\}$} \begin{algorithmic} \REQUIRE Training data $\{(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_n), \Delta\mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_n; \mathbf{x}^{(i)}(t_n))): i=1,\cdots, H, n=0, \cdots, N_T - 1\}$, score networks $\{s_{\theta_n}\}_{n=0}^{N_T - 1}$, batch size $m\le H$, learning rate function $\alpha(\cdot)$, noise schedulers $f(\tau)$ and $g(\tau)$, diffusion horizon $T_g$, number of diffusion steps $K$, diffusion time step $\Delta\tau = T_g/K$ \FOR{episode $j = 1,..., J$} \FOR{SDE slot $t_n= 0, \Delta t, 2\Delta t, ..., (N_T - 1)\Delta t$} \STATE 1. Randomly sample a batch of data at $t_n$: \vspace{-2mm} $$\big\{(\mathbf{c}^{(i_l)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i_l)}(0)) = ((t_n, \mathbf{x}^{(i_l)}(t_n)), \Delta\mathbf{x}^{(i_l)}(t_n; \mathbf{x}^{(i_l)}(t_n))): l=1,\cdots, m\big\}$$ \vspace{-7mm} \STATE 2. Randomly sample a diffusion step $k\sim \text{Unif}[1, K]$ and set $\tau_k = k\Delta\tau$ \STATE 3. Generate noised samples $\{\mathbf{y}^{(i_l)}(\tau_k): l=1,\cdots, m\}$, where \vspace{-3mm} \[\mathbf{y}^{(i_l)}(\tau_k) = e^{-\int_0^{\tau_k} f(v)\mathrm{d} v}\mathbf{y}^{i_l}(0) + \bigg(\int_{0}^{\tau_k} e^{-\int_u^{\tau_k} 2f(v)\mathrm{d} v}g^2(u) \mathrm{d} u\bigg)^{1/2}\zeta_l,\ \zeta_l\sim\mathcal{N}(0, I_d) \] \vspace{-5mm} \STATE 4. Compute the denosing score matching loss $L(\theta_n)$\footnotemark: \vspace{-2mm} \begin{align*} \frac{1}{m}\sum_{l=1}^m \int_{0}^{\tau_k} e^{-\int_u^{\tau_k} 2f(v)\mathrm{d} v}g^2(u) \mathrm{d} u\cdot\big\| s_{\theta_n}(\tau_k, \mathbf{y}^{(i_l)}(\tau_k), \mathbf{c}^{(i_l)}) - \nabla\log q_{\tau_k|0}(\mathbf{y}^{(i_l)}(\tau_k) | \mathbf{y}^{(i_l)}(0), \mathbf{c}^{(i_l)})\big\|^2 \end{align*} \vspace{-4mm} \STATE 5. Update $\theta_n \leftarrow \theta_n - \alpha(j)\nabla_{\theta_n} L(\theta_n)$ \ENDFOR \ENDFOR \RETURN score network $s_{\theta_n}$ of $G(t_n, \cdot; \theta_n)$ for $n=0, \cdots, N_T-1$ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.section: 2.3 Generation of SDE Paths via Conditional Diffusion Models
nodes.label: alg: training_process

nodes.name: Generation of synthetic SDE paths
nodes.statement_short: Autoregressively sample each increment by running the reverse conditional diffusion conditioned on the current time and state.
nodes.statement: \small \caption{Generation of synthetic SDE paths} \begin{algorithmic} \REQUIRE network $\{s_{\theta_n}\}_{n=0}^{N_T - 1}$, initial position $\hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}(0)$, noise schedulers $f(\tau)$ and $g(\tau)$, diffusion horizon $T_g$, number of diffusion steps $K$, diffusion time step $\Delta\tau = T_g/K$ \FOR{SDE slot $t_n= 0, \Delta t, 2\Delta t, ..., (N_T - 1)\Delta t$} \STATE 1. Set the condition $\mathbf{c}_n = (t_n, \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_n))$ \STATE 2. Simulate $\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(\tau_0)\sim\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ \STATE 3. Simulate the reverse process of the conditional diffusion model: \FOR{diffusion step $\tau_k = 0, \Delta\tau, 2\Delta\tau, \cdots, K\Delta\tau$} \vspace{-5mm} \STATE \[\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(\tau_{k + 1}) = \tilde{\mathbf{y}}(\tau_{k}) + [ f(T_g -\tau_{k})\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(\tau_{k}) + g^2(T_g -\tau_{k}) s_{\theta_n}(T_g - \tau_k, \tilde{\mathbf{y}}(\tau_{k}), \mathbf{c}_n)]\Delta\tau + g(T_g - \tau_k) \sqrt{\Delta\tau}\zeta_k \] where $\zeta_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ \ENDFOR \STATE 4. Set and store the next state $\hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_{n + 1}) = \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_n) + \tilde{\mathbf{y}}(\tau_{K})$ \ENDFOR \RETURN generated path $(\hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_0), \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_1), \cdots, \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_{N_T}))$ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.section: 2.3 Generation of SDE Paths via Conditional Diffusion Models
nodes.label: alg: generation_process

nodes.name: Example 1: one-dimensional OU process
nodes.statement: A (one-dimensional) time-homogeneous OU process is governed by \begin{align} \mathrm{d} X(t) = \theta (\mu - X(t)) \mathrm{d} t + \sigma \mathrm{d} W(t),\ X(0) = x(0). \end{align} Set $x(0) = 1.5, \mu=1.2, \theta = 1, \sigma=0.3$, and $T = 1, \Delta t = 0.05$, resulting in $N_T = 20$ observation slots in total. We collect $H = 100$ ``real'' OU trajectories in the training dataset \eqref{eq: obs_data}, each simulated from \eqref{eq: SDE_OU} via Monte Carlo. Then, in each experiment, we generate 100 synthetic OU paths with each of the three methods, and compute the corresponding KL divergences between the joint distributions of the (discrete observations of) 100 real and synthetic paths using the method from \cite{wang2009divergence}. We repeat 5,000 such experiments.

nodes.name: Eq. (9): SDE OU
nodes.statement: \mathrm{d} X(t) = \theta (\mu - X(t)) \mathrm{d} t + \sigma \mathrm{d} W(t),\ X(0) = x(0).
nodes.label: eq: SDE_OU

nodes.name: Example 2: time-inhomogeneous GBM on a non-uniform grid
nodes.statement: A (one-dimensional) time-inhomogeneous GBM is driven by the following SDE: \begin{align} dX(t) = \mu(t)X(t) dt + \sigma(t)X(t) dW(t),\ X(0) = x(0), \end{align} where we choose $\mu(t) = 4t, \sigma(t) = \sqrt{4t}$ and $x(0) = 1$. In this example, we set $T=\frac{1}{2}$ and consider a non-uniform time grid $\mathcal{T}$ to demonstrate the flexibility and generalizability of our approach. Specifically, we generate $N_T=100$ observation time points \textit{at random} on $[0,T]$, and simulate $H=100$ trajectories of \eqref{eq: SDE_TGBM} on $\mathcal{T}$ to construct the training dataset.

nodes.name: Eq. (10): SDE TGBM
nodes.statement: dX(t) = \mu(t)X(t) dt + \sigma(t)X(t) dW(t),\ X(0) = x(0),
nodes.label: eq: SDE_TGBM

nodes.name: Example 3: CIR process
nodes.statement: A (one-dimensional) time-homogeneous Cox–Ingersoll–Ross (CIR) process is \begin{align*} dX(t) = \alpha(b - X(t))dt + \sigma\sqrt{X(t)}dW(t),\ X(0) = x(0). \end{align*} We take $x(0) = 0.5, \alpha = 0.2, b = 0.05, \sigma=0.1$ and the training data are $H=100$ real CIR paths with $T=0.5$ and $\Delta t= 0.01$.

nodes.name: Example 4: 100-dimensional GBM
nodes.statement: A multivariate GBM in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with $d=100$ is defined as: \begin{align*} \mathrm{d}\mathbf{X}_j(t) = \mu_j\mathbf{X}_j(t)\mathrm{d} t + \sigma_j\mathbf{X}_j(t) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}_j(t),\ \mathbf{X}_j(0) = x_j(0),\quad j=1,\cdots, 100, \end{align*} where $\mathbf{W}_j$ is a one-dimensional standard Brownian motion, and $\mathbf{W}_j(t)$ and $\mathbf{W}_l(t)$ have a correlation $\rho_{jl}\in[-1, 1]$ for $j, l=1,..., 100$. We randomly generate $\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\sigma}, \boldsymbol{\rho}$, the corresponding vector or matrices consisting of those model parameters. Set $T=7$ and $\Delta t=1$ so that the time step is ``large''. We use $H=10,000$ real paths to train the three generative models.

nodes.name: Empirical superiority over SDM-MC and Neural SDE
conclusions: our approach consistently outperforms the two benchmarks across nearly all experiments in generating synthetic SDE paths
nodes.statement: In summary, our approach consistently outperforms the two benchmarks across nearly all experiments in generating synthetic SDE paths.

nodes.name: Joint path distributions of target and generated paths
nodes.statement: Given a fixed $\mathbf{X}(t_0) \equiv \mathbf{x}(0)$, we denote by $P_{1:N_T|0}$ the joint distribution of the target path $(\mathbf{X}(t_1), \cdots, \mathbf{X}(t_{N_T}))$, and by $\hat P_{1:N_T|0}$ that of the generated path $(\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_1), \cdots, \hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_{N_T}))$.

nodes.name: Lipschitz/linear-growth coefficients and positive transition densities
nodes.statement: (a) The coefficients $\mu$ and $\sigma$ of the target SDE \eqref{eq: target_SDE} satisfy the global Lipschitz and linear growth conditions: \begin{align*} ||\mu(t, \mathbf{x}) - \mu(t, \mathbf{x}')||_2 + ||\sigma(t, \mathbf{x}) - \sigma(t, \mathbf{x}')||_2 &\le C_L||\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'||_2,\\ ||\mu(t, \mathbf{x})||_2 + ||\sigma(t, \mathbf{x})||_2 &\le C_L(1 + ||\mathbf{x}||_2), \end{align*} for every $t\in[0, T], \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d, \mathbf{x}'\in\mathbb{R}^d$, where $C_L$ is a positive constant independent of $(t, \mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')$. (b) For any $0 \le s \le t \le T$, the conditional distribution of $\mathbf{X}(t)$ given $\mathbf{X}(s) = \mathbf{x}(s)$ is absolutely continuous w.r.t. the Lebesgue measure, and it admits a probability density function that is positive almost everywhere on $\mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.label: assumption: SDE_solution_supp_abs

nodes.name: Existence and uniqueness of strong solutions
nodes.statement: Assumption \ref{assumption: SDE_solution_supp_abs}(a) is the classical (sufficient) condition for a general SDE to have a unique strong solution \citep{karatzas2014brownian}.

nodes.name: Moment bounds for SDE solutions (Kloeden-Platen Thm 4.5.4)
assumptions: under this assumption
conclusions: $$\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{X}(t)\|^2 \le (1 + \mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{X}(0)\|^2)e^{tC_M}$$
nodes.statement_short: Second moments of the solution grow at most exponentially and increment second moments are $O(\Delta t)$.
nodes.statement: Moreover, under this assumption the solution to \eqref{eq: target_SDE} admits the following moment bounds \citep[Theorem 4.5.4]{kloedennumerical}: there exists a positive constant $C_M$ depending only on $C_L$ such that $$\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{X}(t)\|^2 \le (1 + \mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{X}(0)\|^2)e^{tC_M}$$ for any $t\in[0, T],$ and \begin{align} \mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{X}(t_{n + 1}) - \mathbf{X}(t_n)\|^2 &\le M_2(t_n; T) \cdot e^{\Delta tC_M}\Delta t \end{align} for any $t_n\in\mathcal{T}$, where \begin{align*} M_2(t_n; T)&:= D_1 \cdot (T - t_n + 1)(1 + \mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{X}(t_n)\|^2) \nonumber \\ & \le D_2\cdot (T - t_n + 1)(1 + \mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{X}(0)\|^2)e^{t_{n}C_M }, \end{align*} and $D_1$ and $D_2$ are some positive constants depending only on $C_L$.

nodes.name: Eq. (11): target SDE moment bound
nodes.statement: \mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{X}(t_{n + 1}) - \mathbf{X}(t_n)\|^2 &\le M_2(t_n; T) \cdot e^{\Delta tC_M}\Delta t
nodes.label: eq: target_SDE_moment_bound

nodes.name: Conditional increment distribution
nodes.statement: For any $t_n\in\mathcal{T}$, denote by $P_{\Delta\mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))}$ the conditional distribution of the increment $\Delta\mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))$ of the target SDE given $\mathbf{X}(t_n) = \mathbf{x}(t_n)\in\mathbb{R}^d$.

nodes.name: Generated increment and its distribution

If Assumption \ref{assumption: score_matching_error} holds for the conditional diffusion model $G(t_n, \cdot; \theta_n)$ at each $t_n\in\mathcal{T}$, then \begin{align*} &\text{KL}(P_{1:N_T|0} || \hat P_{1:N_T|0}) \\ & \lesssim \sum_{n=0}^{N_T - 1} \bigg\{\underbrace{e^{-\frac{a}{2}T_g^2(t_n) - bT_g(t_n)}\big[M_2(t_{n}; T) e^{\Delta tC_M}\Delta t + de^{-\frac{a}{2}T_g^2(t_n) - bT_g(t_n)}\big]}_{initialization\ error} + \underbrace{[T_g(t_n) + 1]^3\varepsilon_{\text{score}}^2}_{score\ matching\ error} \\ &\quad \qquad \quad+ \underbrace{\frac{1}{K_n}\big(M_2(t_{n}; T) e^{\Delta tC_M}\Delta t + d\big)(T_g(t_n) + 1)^6 + \frac{d \cdot T_g(t_n) \cdot L_1(t_n)}{K_n}}_{discretization\ error}\bigg\}, \end{align*} where $\Delta t$ is the time step of observing \eqref{eq: target_SDE}, $M_2(t_n; T)$ and $C_M$ are defined in \eqref{eq: target_SDE_moment_bound}, and $T_g(t_n)=K_n\Delta\tau_n$ is the diffusion time horizon of $G(t_n, \mathbf{x}; \theta_n)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm: SDE_diffusion_convergence} directly follows from Proposition~\ref{prop: path_KL_decomposition}, Proposition~\ref{prop: condition_diffusion_KL_bound} and the moment bound of the SDE increment in \eqref{eq: target_SDE_moment_bound}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement_short: Show each transition and path law is equivalent to Lebesgue via positivity of densities and the Markov factorization, then apply the KL chain rule.
nodes.statement: Throughout this proof, if a probability distribution is absolutely continuous w.r.t the Lebesgue measure, we simply say this distribution is ACL. We first consider the target paths. For any $t_n\in\mathcal{T}$, denote by $P_{n + 1| n}(\cdot | \mathbf{x}(t_n))$ the conditional distribution of $\mathbf{X}(t_{n + 1})$ given $\mathbf{X}(t_n) = \mathbf{x}(t_n)$, which is ACL and positive almost everywhere on $\mathbb{R}^d$ according to Assumption \ref{assumption: SDE_solution_supp_abs}(b). It follows that the conditional distribution $P_{\Delta\mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))}$ of the increment is also ACL and positive almost everywhere on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Therefore, for any $A\subset \mathbb{R}^d$, \begin{align} \int_{\mathbf{x}\in A}1 \mathrm{d} \mathbf{x} = 0\quad \text{ if and only if }\quad \int_{\mathbf{x} \in A}1\cdot \frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\Delta\mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))}(\mathbf{x})}{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \mathrm{d} \mathbf{x}= 0, \end{align} where $\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\Delta\mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))}(\mathbf{x})}{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{x}}$ is the Radon–Nikodym derivative (i.e., the density function) of $P_{\Delta\mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))}(\mathbf{x})$ w.r.t. the Lebesgue measure. This implies that $P_{\Delta\mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))}$ and the Lebesgue measure are equivalent. Next, consider $P_{1:N_T|0}$. For any $0 \le m < n\le N_T$, let $\mathbf{X}(m:n):=(\mathbf{X}(t_m), \mathbf{X}(t_{m + 1}),\cdots, \mathbf{X}(t_n))$, and denote by $P_{m:n|0}$ the joint distribution of $\mathbf{X}(m:n)$ conditional on $\mathbf{X}(t_0)\equiv\mathbf{x}(t_0)$. Let $\mathbf{x}(m:n) = (\mathbf{x}(t_m), \cdots, \mathbf{x}(t_n))$ be a realization of $\mathbf{X}(m:n)$. Due to the Markov property of the Target SDE \eqref{eq: target_SDE}, we have \begin{align} \mathrm{d} P_{m:n|0}(\mathbf{x}(m:n)) &= \mathrm{d} \bigg[P_{m|0}(\mathbf{x}(t_m))\prod_{j=m}^{n - 1}P\big(\mathbf{X}(t_{j + 1})=\mathbf{x}(t_{j + 1}) | \mathbf{X}(m:j)=\mathbf{x}(m:j)\big)\bigg] \nonumber\\ &= \mathrm{d} \bigg[P_{m|0}(\mathbf{x}(t_m))\prod_{j=m}^{n - 1}P\big(\mathbf{X}(t_{j + 1})=\mathbf{x}(t_{j + 1}) | \mathbf{X}(t_j)=\mathbf{x}(t_j)\big)\bigg] \nonumber\\ &= \mathrm{d} P_{m|0}(\mathbf{x}(t_m))\prod_{j=m}^{n - 1}\mathrm{d} P_{j + 1 | j}\big(\mathbf{x}(t_{j + 1}) | \mathbf{x}(t_j)\big), \end{align} where we recall that $P_{m|0}(\mathbf{x}(t_m))$ and $P_{j + 1 | j}\big(\mathbf{x}(t_{j + 1}) | \mathbf{x}(t_j)\big)$ are ACL and positive almost everywhere on $\mathbb{R}^d$ for any $m$ and $j$ because of Assumption \ref{assumption: SDE_solution_supp_abs}(b). Hence, $P_{m:n|0}$ is ACL and positive almost everywhere on $\mathbb{R}^{d\times (n - m + 1)}$ for any $m < n$. In particular, $P_{1:N_T|0}$ is ACL and positive almost everywhere on $\mathbb{R}^{d\times N_T}$. Using a similar argument as in \eqref{eq: equivalent_to_lebesgue}, we deduce that $P_{1:N_T|0}$ is equivalent to the Lebesgue measure. On the other hand, consider the distribution of the generated increment $\hat P_{\Delta\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))}$ for a given $t_n$ and $\mathbf{x}(t_n)$. Note that $\Delta\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))$ is the terminal state (i.e. $\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_K)$) at the last step of the generation process \eqref{eq: reverse_SDE_DDPM_simulation}, which means it is the sum of a random variable determined by the state of the second last step of \eqref{eq: reverse_SDE_DDPM_simulation} (i.e. $ \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}(\tau_{K - 1})$) and an independent Gaussian variable (with mean $0$ and variance $g^2(T_g - \tau_{K - 1})\Delta\tau \cdot I_d$). It follows that $\hat P_{\Delta\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))}$ is ACL and positive almost everywhere on $\mathbb{R}^d$ by Corollary 2.2 of \cite{bhattacharya2007basic}, and consequently also equivalent to the Lebesgue measure for each $n$. By the autoregressive generation \eqref{eq: AR_generation}, the conditional distribution $\hat P_{n + 1|n}(\cdot |\hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_n))$ of $\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_{n + 1})$ conditional on $\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_n)=\hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_n)$ is ACL and positive almost everywhere on $\mathbb{R}^d$ for each $n$. Using similar arguments leading to \eqref{eq: equivalent_to_lebesgue} and \eqref{eq: target_Markov}, we conclude that the distribution $\hat P_{1:N_T|0}$ of the entire generated path $\big(\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_1, \cdots, \hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_{N_T})\big)$ is equivalent to the Lebesgue measure and positive almost everywhere on $\mathbb{R}^{d\times N_T}$. Finally, we establish the decomposition result \eqref{eq: path_KL_decomposition} for the KL-divergence between the target and generated paths. Note that given $\mathbf{X}(t_0)\equiv \mathbf{x}(t_0)$, the Markov property holds for both $\mathbf{X}(1:N_T)$ and $\hat{\mathbf{X}}(1:N_T)$. Then, the chain rule of KL-divergence \citep[Exercise 3.2]{wainwright2019high} implies that \begin{align*} \text{KL}\big(P_{1:N_T|0} || \hat P_{1:N_T|0}\big) &= \sum_{n=0}^{N_T - 1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}(0:n)\sim \mathbf{X}(0:n)| \mathbf{X}(t_0)} \bigg[\text{KL}\big(P_{\mathbf{X}(t_{n + 1}) |\mathbf{X}(0:n)=\mathbf{x}(0:n)} \big|\big| \hat P_{\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_{n + 1}) |\hat{\mathbf{X}}(0:n)=\mathbf{x}(0:n)}\bigg]\\ &=\sum_{n=0}^{N_T - 1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}(0:n)\sim \mathbf{X}(0:n)| \mathbf{X}(t_0)} \bigg[\text{KL}\big(P_{\mathbf{X}(t_{n + 1}) |\mathbf{X}(t_n)=\mathbf{x}(t_n)} \big|\big| \hat P_{\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_{n + 1}) |\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_n)=\mathbf{x}(t_n)}\bigg]\\ &= \sum_{n=0}^{N_T - 1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}(t_n)\sim \mathbf{X}(t_n)| \mathbf{X}(t_0)} \bigg[\text{KL}\big(P_{\Delta\mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))} \big|\big| \hat P_{\Delta\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_n; \mathbf{x}(t_n))}\bigg]\\ &= \sum_{n=0}^{N_T - 1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}(t_n)\sim P_{n|0}}\bigg[\text{KL}\big(P_{\Delta\mathbf{X}(t_n; \mathbf{X}(t_n))} \big|\big| \hat P_{\Delta\hat{\mathbf{X}}(t_n; \mathbf{X}(t_n))}\big)\bigg]. \end{align*} This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Gaussian transition of the forward OU process
nodes.statement_short: Under the linear schedule the forward process transition from $\tau$ to $s$ is an explicit scaled-plus-Gaussian-noise map.
nodes.statement: The forward equation \eqref{eq: forward_SDE_DDPM} admits an analytical solution \begin{align} \mathbf{Y}(s) &= e^{-\int_\tau^sf(v)\mathrm{d} v}\mathbf{Y}(\tau) + \int_{\tau}^s e^{-\int_u^sf(v)\mathrm{d} v}g(u) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{B}(u) \nonumber \\ & \overset{d}{=} e^{-\frac{a}{4}(s^2 - \tau^2) - \frac{b}{2}(s - \tau)}\mathbf{Y}(\tau) + \sqrt{1 - e^{-\frac{a}{2}(s^2 - \tau^2) - b(s - \tau)}}\cdot\zeta, \end{align} for any $0 < \tau < s < T_g$, where $\zeta\sim\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ is independent of $\mathbf{Y}(\tau)$.

nodes.name: Eq. (21): DDPM conditional relation
nodes.statement: \mathbf{Y}(s) &= e^{-\int_\tau^sf(v)\mathrm{d} v}\mathbf{Y}(\tau) + \int_{\tau}^s e^{-\int_u^sf(v)\mathrm{d} v}g(u) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{B}(u) \nonumber \\ & \overset{d}{=} e^{-\frac{a}{4}(s^2 - \tau^2) - \frac{b}{2}(s - \tau)}\mathbf{Y}(\tau) + \sqrt{1 - e^{-\frac{a}{2}(s^2 - \tau^2) - b(s - \tau)}}\cdot\zeta,
nodes.label: eq: DDPM_conditional_relation

nodes.name: Forward coefficients $\lambda_{\tau,s}$ and $\sigma^2_{\tau,s}$
nodes.statement: Let \begin{align} \lambda_{\tau, s} := e^{-\frac{a}{4}(s^2 - \tau^2) - \frac{b}{2}(s - \tau)}, \quad \lambda_\tau:= \lambda_{0,\tau}, \quad \sigma^2_{\tau, s} := 1 - e^{-\frac{a}{2}(s^2 - \tau^2) - b(s - \tau)},\quad \text{and} \quad \sigma_{\tau}^2 = \sigma^2_{0,\tau}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Eq. (22): forward SDE coeff
nodes.statement: \lambda_{\tau, s} := e^{-\frac{a}{4}(s^2 - \tau^2) - \frac{b}{2}(s - \tau)}, \quad \lambda_\tau:= \lambda_{0,\tau}, \quad \sigma^2_{\tau, s} := 1 - e^{-\frac{a}{2}(s^2 - \tau^2) - b(s - \tau)},\quad \text{and} \quad \sigma_{\tau}^2 = \sigma^2_{0,\tau}.

nodes.name: Gaussian transition density $q_{s|\tau}$
nodes.statement: We then have $\mathbf{Y}(s) | \mathbf{Y}(\tau) \sim \mathcal{N}(\lambda_{\tau, s}\mathbf{Y}(\tau), \sigma^2_{\tau, s}I_d)$, and we denote by $q_{s|\tau}(\cdot | \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{c})$ the corresponding Gaussian density when $\mathbf{Y}(\tau) = \mathbf{y}$ under the conditional $\mathbf{c}$.

nodes.name: Overview of the proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the KL into initialization, discretization and score-matching terms (Lemma 1) and bound each with Lemmas 2-5.
nodes.statement:
Given a fixed condition $\mathbf{c}$, we first state Lemma ef{lemma: KL_bound_decomposition} below, which decomposes $	ext{KL} ig(p_{	ext{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_K}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) ig)$ and identifies various sources of approximation errors.  egin{lemma} For a given condition $\mathbf{c}$, denote by $	ilde p^	heta_{	au_K}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$ the marginal density of the generated $	ilde{\mathbf{Z}}(	au_K)$ of the reverse process \eqref{eq: reverse_SDE_DDPM_simulation}. Under the conditions of Proposition ef{prop: condition_diffusion_KL_bound}, we have  egin{align} &	ext{KL} ig(p_{	ext{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_K}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) ig) 
onumber\ &\lesssim 	ext{KL} ig(q_{T_g}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || \mathcal{N}(0, I_d) ig) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \int_{	au_{k-1}}^{	au_k}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_	au(\cdot | \mathbf{c}), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k|	au}(\cdot |\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{c})} ig[||f(	au)\mathbf{Y}(	au) - f(	au_k)\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)||^2 ig]\mathrm{d}	au 
onumber\ &\qquad + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \int_{	au_{k-1}}^{	au_k}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_	au(\cdot | \mathbf{c}), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k | 	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{c})} ig[||g^2(	au)
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c})||^2 ig]\mathrm{d}	au
onumber\ &\qquad + \sum_{k=1}^{K}\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_{k}}[g^2(	au_k) - g^2(	au)]^2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_{	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}  ig[ ig\|
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) ig\|^2 ig] \mathrm{d}	au 
onumber \ &\qquad + \Delta 	au\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim q_{	au_k}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})} ig[||g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)s_	heta(	au_k, \mathbf{Y}(	au_k), \mathbf{c})||^2 ig]. \end{align} \end{lemma} The proof of Lemma ef{lemma: KL_bound_decomposition} can be found in Appendix ef{sec: error_identification}. We next discuss how to bound each term on the right-hand-side of \eqref{eq: KL_bound_decomposition}. The first term of \eqref{eq: KL_bound_decomposition} is the initialization error arising from the use of the Gaussian noise, instead of the terminal state of the forward process, as the initialization of the generation process \eqref{eq: reverse_SDE_DDPM_simulation}. We bound this initialization error in Lemma ef{lemma: initial_dist_error_bound}, leveraging on the exponential convergence property of the forward OU process \eqref{eq: forward_SDE_DDPM}. The proof of Lemma~ef{lemma: initial_dist_error_bound} is given in Appendix ef{sec: Gaussian_initialization_error}.  egin{lemma} For the terminal marginal density $q_{T_g}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$ induced by the forward process defined in \eqref{eq: forward_SDE_DDPM}, if the moment condition \eqref{eq: convergence_finite_moment} is satisfied, then we have:  egin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[	ext{KL} ig(q_{T_g}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || \mathcal{N}(0, I_d) ig) igg]\lesssim e^{- rac{a}{2}T_g^2 - bT_g} ig[M_2 + de^{- rac{a}{2}T_g^2 - bT_g} ig]. \end{align*} \end{lemma} Next, we bound the second term of \eqref{eq: KL_bound_decomposition}, which accounts for the state discretization error of using $f(	au_k)\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)$ to approximate $f(	au)\mathbf{Y}(	au)$ for $	au\in[	au_{k - 1}, 	au_k]$. Lemma ef{lemma: state_discrete_error_bound} shows that this error can be controlled under the finite moment condition \eqref{eq: convergence_finite_moment}. The proof, deferred to Appendix ef{sec: state_discrretization_error}, is based on applying It\^{o}'s formula to $f(	au)\mathbf{Y}(	au)$.  egin{lemma} For the forward process $\mathbf{Y}$ in \eqref{eq: forward_SDE_DDPM}, if the moment condition \eqref{eq: convergence_finite_moment} is satisfied, then we have:  egin{align*} &\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[\sum_{k=1}^{K} \int_{	au_{k -1}}^{	au_k}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_	au(\cdot | \mathbf{c}), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k | 	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{c})} ig[||f(	au)\mathbf{Y}(	au) - f(	au_k)\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)||^2 ig]\mathrm{d}	au igg] \ &\lesssim \Delta	au(M_2 + d)(T_g + 1)^5. \end{align*} \end{lemma} The third error term in \eqref{eq: KL_bound_decomposition} represents the time and space discretization error for approximating the score function $g^2(	au)
abla\log q_{	au}(\mathbf{Y}(	au)|\mathbf{c})$ by $g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)| \mathbf{c})$ when $	au\in[	au_{k - 1}, 	au_k]$. We bound this error in Lemma ef{lemma: score_discretization_error_bound}. Our proof is inspired by that of Theorem 5 of \cite{chen2023improved}, but we improve their dependence on the data dimension $d$ by applying the stochastic localization technique introduced in \cite{bentonnearly}; see Appendix ef{sec: score_discretization_error} for the complete proof.  egin{lemma} Suppose the first condition of Proposition~ef{prop: condition_diffusion_KL_bound} holds. Then for the forward process $\{\mathbf{Y}(	au): 	au\in[0, T_g]\}$ in \eqref{eq: forward_SDE_DDPM} and the corresponding score function $\{
abla\log q_	au(\cdot | \mathbf{c}): 	au\in[0, T_g]\}$, we have  egin{align*} &\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[\sum_{k=1}^{K}\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_{k}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_{	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}),\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k | 	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{c})}[ ig\| g^2(	au)
abla\log q_{	au}(\mathbf{Y}(	au)|\mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)| \mathbf{c})  ig\|]^2\mathrm{d} 	au igg]\ &\lesssim M_2\Delta	au (T_g + 1)^2 + d\Delta	au  ig[L_1 + (T_g + 1)^4  ig]. \end{align*} \end{lemma} The fourth term of \eqref{eq: KL_bound_decomposition} is the discretization error of simulating the Brownian motion $g(	au)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}(	au)$ in \eqref{eq: reverse_SDE_DDPM} by $g(	au_k)\sqrt{\Delta	au}\zeta_k \overset{d}{=}g(	au_k)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}(	au)$ from $	au_k$ to $	au_{k + 1}$ in \eqref{eq: reverse_SDE_DDPM_simulation}. We provide a bound on this error in Lemma ef{lemma: BM_discretization_error_bound}, whose proof is given in Appendix ef{sec: BM_discrete_error}.  egin{lemma} Under the same condition as in Lemma~ef{lemma: score_discretization_error_bound}, we have  egin{align*} &\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[\sum_{k=1}^{K}\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_{k}}[g^2(	au_k) - g^2(	au)]^2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_{	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}  ig[ ig\|
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) ig\|^2 ig] \mathrm{d}	au igg]\ & \quad \lesssim d(\Delta	au)^2[L_1 + T_g + 1]. \end{align*} \end{lemma} The last term of \eqref{eq: KL_bound_decomposition} captures the score matching error out of the neural network approximation of the true score function. Given condition \eqref{eq: convergence_score_matching}, we have  egin{align} &\Delta 	au\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim q_{	au_k}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})} ig[||g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)s_	heta(	au_k, \mathbf{Y}(	au_k), \mathbf{c})||^2 ig] igg]
onumber\ &\le (T_g + 1)^3\varepsilon_{	ext{score}}^2. \end{align} Finally, by combining the results of Lemma ef{lemma: KL_bound_decomposition} through Lemma ef{lemma: BM_discretization_error_bound}, along with the bound \eqref{eq: score_matching_error_bound} on the score matching error, we obtain the error bound in \eqref{eq: condition_diffusion_KL_bound}, proving Proposition ef{prop: condition_diffusion_KL_bound}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement_short: Integrate Lemma 6(b) over each step, average using Lemma 6(a), and chain the per-step KLs by the KL chain rule.
nodes.statement:
We apply the result of Lemma ef{lemma: KL_dt}(b) and set $C_{KL} = b$. Note that $	ilde g^2(	au) = g^2(T_g - 	au) = a(T_g - 	au) + b \ge b$ for any $	au\in[0, T_g]$. Then, integrating on both sides of \eqref{eq: density_KL_dt_bound} from $	au_k$ to $	au_{k + 1}$, we have  egin{align*} &	ext{KL} ig(	ilde p_{	au_{k + 1} | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{z}}) || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_{k + 1} | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{z}} ig) - \lim_{	au	o	au_k+}	ext{KL} ig(	ilde p_{	au | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{z}}) || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{z}} ig)\ &\le  rac{1}{b}\int_{	au_k}^{	au_{k + 1}} \mathbb{E}_{	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)\sim	ilde p_{	au | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{z}})}  ig\|	ilde f(	au)	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au) - 	ilde f(	au_k)	ilde{\mathbf{z}} + 	ilde g^2(	au)
abla\log q_{T_g - 	au}(	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)|\mathbf{c}) - 	ilde g^2(	au_k)s_	heta(T_g - 	au_k, 	ilde{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{c}) ig\|^2\mathrm{d} 	au\ &\qquad +  rac{1}{4b}\int_{	au_k}^{	au_{k + 1}} [	ilde g^2(	au_k) - 	ilde g^2(	au)]^2\mathbb{E}_{	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)\sim	ilde p_{	au | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{z}})}  ig[ ig\|
abla\log	ilde p_	au(	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)) ig\|^2 ig] \mathrm{d}	au. \end{align*} Since the above result holds when $	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)= 	ilde{\mathbf{Z}}(	au_k) = 	ilde {\mathbf{z}}$ for any fixed $	ilde{\mathbf{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^d$, we can integrate on both sides of the above inequality w.r.t. $	ilde {\mathbf{z}} = 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)\sim 	ilde p_{	au_k}$. Then, by Lemma ef{lemma: KL_dt}(a), we have  egin{align} &\mathbb{E}_{	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)\sim 	ilde p_{	au_k}}  ig[	ext{KL} ig(	ilde p_{	au_{k + 1} | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)) || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_{k +1} | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k) ig)  ig] 
onumber\ &\le  rac{1}{b}\int_{	au_k}^{	au_{k + 1}}\mathbb{E}_{(	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k), 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au))} igg[ ig\|	ilde g^2(	au)
abla\log q_{T_g - 	au}(	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)|\mathbf{c}) - 	ilde g^2(	au_k)s_	heta(T_g - 	au_k, 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k), \mathbf{c}) 
onumber\ &\qquad \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad + 	ilde f(	au)	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au) - 	ilde f(	au_k) 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)  ig\|^2 igg]\mathrm{d} 	au
onumber\ &\qquad +  rac{1}{4b}\int_{	au_k}^{	au_{k + 1}} [	ilde g^2(	au_k) - 	ilde g^2(	au)]^2\mathbb{E}_{	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)\sim 	ilde p_	au}  ig[ ig\|
abla\log	ilde p_	au(	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)) ig\|^2 ig] \mathrm{d}	au, \end{align} where the expectation in the first term on the right-hand side is taken w.r.t. $	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)\sim	ilde p_{	au_k}$ and $	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)\sim	ilde p_{	au|	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k))$. On the other hand, consider the reverse SDE \eqref{eq: piece_reverse_SDE} starting from $	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)\sim	ilde p_{	au_k}$, and the simulated SDE \eqref{eq: piece_reverse_SDE_simulation} starting from $	ilde{\mathbf{Z}}(	au_k)\sim	ilde p^	heta_{t_k}$. Using the chain rule of KL divergence, we have the following result:  egin{equation} 	ext{KL} ig(	ilde p_{	au_{k + 1}} || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_{k + 1}} ig) \le 	ext{KL} ig(	ilde p_{	au_{k}} || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_{k}} ig) + \mathbb{E}_{	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)\sim	ilde p_{	au_k}} ig[	ext{KL} ig(	ilde p_{	au_{k + 1} | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)) || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_{k + 1} | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k) ig)  ig]. \end{equation} With \eqref{eq: DDPM_simulation_step_bound} and \eqref{eq: KL_chain_rule}, we have  egin{align*} &	ext{KL}(p_{	ext{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_K}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})) = 	ext{KL}(q_0(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_K}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})) = 	ext{KL} ig(	ilde p_{T_g} || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_K} ig) = 	ext{KL} ig(	ilde p_{	au_K} || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_K} ig)\ &\overset{\eqref{eq: KL_chain_rule}}{\le} 	ext{KL} ig(	ilde p_0 || 	ilde p^	heta_0 ig) + \sum_{k = 0}^{K - 1}\mathbb{E}_{	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)\sim	ilde p_{	au_k}} ig[	ext{KL} ig(	ilde p_{	au_{k + 1} | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)) || 	ilde p^	heta_{	au_{k + 1} | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k) ig)  ig]\ &\overset{\eqref{eq: DDPM_simulation_step_bound}}{\le} 	ext{KL} ig(q_{T_g}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || \mathcal{N}(0, I_d) ig) +  rac{1}{4b}\sum_{k=0}^{K - 1}\int_{	au_k}^{	au_{k + 1}}[	ilde g^2(	au_k) - 	ilde g^2(	au)]^2\mathbb{E}_{	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)\sim	ilde p_{	au}}  ig[ ig\|
abla\log	ilde p_	au(	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)) ig\|^2 ig] \mathrm{d}	au\ &\qquad +  rac{1}{b}\sum_{k = 0}^{K - 1}\int_{	au_k}^{	au_{k + 1}}\mathbb{E}_{	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k)\sim	ilde p_{	au_k},	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)\sim	ilde p_{	au | 	au_k}(\cdot | 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k))} igg[ ig\|	ilde g^2(	au)
abla\log q_{T_g - 	au}(	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au)|\mathbf{c}) - 	ilde g^2(	au_k)s_	heta(T_g - 	au_k, 	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k), \mathbf{c}) \ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad + 	ilde f(	au)	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au) - 	ilde f(	au_k)	ilde{\mathbf{Y}}(	au_k) ig\|^2 igg]\mathrm{d} 	au\ &\le 	ext{KL} ig(q_{T_g}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || \mathcal{N}(0, I_d) ig) +  rac{1}{4b}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_{k}}[g^2(	au_k) - g^2(	au)]^2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_{	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}  ig[ ig\|
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) ig\|^2 ig] \mathrm{d}	au\ &\qquad +  rac{1}{b}\sum_{k = 1}^{K}\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_{k}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_{	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}),\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k | 	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(	au_k), \mathbf{c})} igg[ ig\|g^2(	au)
abla\log q_{	au}(\mathbf{Y}(	au)|\mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)s_	heta(	au_k, \mathbf{Y}(	au_k), \mathbf{c}) \ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad + f(	au)\mathbf{Y}(	au) - f(	au_k)\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) ig\|^2 igg]\mathrm{d} 	au\ &\lesssim 	ext{KL} ig(q_{T_g}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || \mathcal{N}(0, I_d) ig) + \sum_{k=1}^{K}\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_{k}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_{	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}),\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k | 	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(	au_k), \mathbf{c})} ig[ ig\|f(	au_k)\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) - f(	au)\mathbf{Y}(	au)  ig\|^2 ig] \mathrm{d} 	au\ &\qquad + \sum_{k=1}^{K}\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_{k}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_{	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}),\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k | 	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(	au_k), \mathbf{c})} ig[ ig\| g^2(	au)
abla\log q_{	au}(\mathbf{Y}(	au)|\mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)| \mathbf{c})  ig\| ig]^2\mathrm{d} 	au\ &\qquad + \sum_{k=1}^{K}\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_{k}}[g^2(	au_k) - g^2(	au)]^2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_{	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}  ig[ ig\|
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) ig\|^2 ig] \mathrm{d}	au\ &\qquad + \Delta	au\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}  ig\| g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)|\mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)s_	heta(	au_k, \mathbf{Y}(	au_k), \mathbf{c})  ig\|^2, \end{align*} where the last step is obtained by adding and subtracting a term of $g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c})$, and using the fact that $\|\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{z}\|^2 \le 9\|\mathbf{x}\|^2 + 9\|\mathbf{y}\|^2 + 9\|\mathbf{z}\|^2$. The proof is hence completed.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement_short: Compute the Gaussian KL explicitly and use convexity of KL (Jensen) with the second-moment bound.
nodes.statement: We adapt the proof of Proposition 4 of \cite{bentonnearly} to our setting where the forward OU process is time-inhomogeneous. Recall that $q_{\tau | 0}(\cdot | \mathbf{y}(0), \mathbf{c})$ is the conditional distribution of $\mathbf{Y}(\tau)$ given $\mathbf{Y}(0) = \mathbf{y}(0)$ under condition $\mathbf{c}$, and $q_{\tau | 0}(\cdot | \mathbf{y}(0), \mathbf{c}) \sim \mathcal{N}(\lambda_\tau \mathbf{Y}(0), \sigma_\tau^2I_d)$ from \eqref{eq: DDPM_conditional_relation} and \eqref{eq: forward_SDE_coeff}. Then, one can directly compute that \begin{align*} \text{KL}(q_{\tau | 0}(\cdot | \mathbf{y}(0), \mathbf{c}) || \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)) = \frac{1}{2}\big(d\log\sigma_\tau^{-2} - d + d\sigma_\tau^2 + \|\lambda_\tau\mathbf{y}(0)\|^2\big). \end{align*} By the convexity of the KL divergence and Jensen's inequality, we have \begin{align*} \text{KL}\big(q_{T_g}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\big) &= \text{KL}\bigg(\int_{\mathbf{y}(0)\in\mathbb{R}^d} q_{T_g | 0}(\cdot | \mathbf{y}(0), \mathbf{c}) \mathrm{d} q_0(\mathbf{y}(0) | \mathbf{c}) \bigg|\bigg| \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\bigg)\\ &\le \int_{\mathbf{y}(0)\in\mathbb{R}^d}\text{KL}\big(q_{T_g | 0}(\cdot | \mathbf{y}(0), \mathbf{c}) || \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\big)\mathrm{d} q_0(\mathbf{y}(0) | \mathbf{c})\\ & =\frac{1}{2}\bigg(d\log\sigma_{T_g}^{-2} - d + d\sigma_{T_g}^2 + \lambda_{T_g}^2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(0)\sim q_{0}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}\|\mathbf{Y}(0)\|^2\bigg)\\ &\lesssim de^{-aT_g^2 - 2bT_g} + e^{-\frac{a}{2}T_g^2 - bT_g}\big(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(0)\sim p_{\text{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}\|\mathbf{Y}(0)\|^2\big) \end{align*} where we use \eqref{eq: forward_SDE_coeff} and the approximation that $-\ln(1 - x)\lesssim x + \frac{x^2}{2}$ for $x\in(-1, 1)$. Applying condition \eqref{eq: convergence_finite_moment}, we immediately obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}}\bigg[\text{KL}\big(q_{T_g}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}) || \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\big)\bigg] \lesssim e^{-\frac{a}{2}T_g^2 - bT_g}\big[M_2 + de^{-\frac{a}{2}T_g^2 - bT_g}\big]. \end{align*} This completes the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: initial_dist_error_bound}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement_short: Apply Ito's formula to $f(\tau)Y(\tau)$, then Cauchy-Schwarz and the second-moment bound.
nodes.statement: By It\^{o}'s formula, with $\mathbf{Y}(\tau)$ following the forward SDE \eqref{eq: forward_SDE_DDPM}, we have \begin{align*} \mathrm{d}(f(\tau)\mathbf{Y}(\tau)) = f'(\tau)\mathbf{Y}(\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau + f(\tau)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{Y}(\tau) = \bigg[\frac{a}{2} - \frac{1}{4}(a\tau + b)^2\bigg]\mathbf{Y}(\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau + \frac{1}{2}(a\tau + b)^{\frac{3}{2}}\mathrm{d} \mathbf{B}(\tau). \end{align*} Let $u(\tau) := \frac{a}{2} - \frac{1}{4}(a\tau + b)^2$ and $v(\tau):=\frac{1}{2}(a\tau + b)^{\frac{3}{2}}$. Then \begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(\tau)\sim q_\tau(\cdot | \mathbf{c}), \mathbf{Y}(\tau_k)\sim q_{\tau_k | \tau}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(\tau), \mathbf{c})}\big[||f(\tau)\mathbf{Y}(\tau) - f(\tau_k)\mathbf{Y}(\tau_k)||^2\big] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(\tau)\sim q_\tau(\cdot | \mathbf{c}), (\mathbf{B})} \bigg[\bigg|\bigg|\int_{\tau}^{\tau_k}u(s)\mathbf{Y}(s)\mathrm{d} s + \int_{\tau}^{\tau_k}v(s)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}(s)\bigg|\bigg|^2\bigg] \\ &\lesssim \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(\tau)\sim q_\tau(\cdot | \mathbf{c}), (\mathbf{B})} \bigg[\bigg|\bigg|\int_{\tau}^{\tau_k}u(s)\mathbf{Y}(s)\mathrm{d} s\bigg|\bigg|^2 + \bigg|\bigg|\int_{\tau}^{\tau_k}v(s)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{B}(s)\bigg|\bigg|^2\bigg] \\ &\lesssim d\int_{\tau}^{\tau_k}v^2(s) \mathrm{d} s+ \left(\int_{\tau}^{\tau_k}u^2(s)\mathrm{d} s\right)\left(\int_{\tau}^{\tau_k}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(s)\sim q_s(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}[||\mathbf{Y}(s)||^2]\mathrm{d} s\right) , \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. Note that $\mathbf{Y}(s) | \mathbf{Y}(0) \sim \mathcal{N}(\lambda_s\mathbf{Y}(0), \sigma_s^2I_d)$ for $\mathbf{Y}(0)\sim p_{\text{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$. Since $\lambda^2_s, \sigma_s^2\le 1$ for any $s\in[0, T_g]$, it follows that \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(s)\sim q_s(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}[||\mathbf{Y}(s)||^2] \le \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(0)\sim p_{\text{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}[\|\mathbf{Y}(0)\|^2 ] + d. \end{align*} Meanwhile, given that $\int_{\tau}^{\tau_k}u^2(s)\mathrm{d} s \lesssim \int_{\tau}^{\tau_k}(s + 1)^4\mathrm{d} s \lesssim (\Delta\tau)(\tau + 1)^4$ and $\int_{\tau}^{\tau_k}v^2(s)\mathrm{d} s \lesssim (\Delta\tau)(\tau + 1)^3$, we derive \begin{align*} & \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}}\bigg[\sum_{k=1}^{K} \int_{\tau_{k - 1}}^{\tau_k} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(\tau)\sim q_\tau(\cdot | \mathbf{c}), \mathbf{Y}(\tau_k)\sim q_{\tau_k | \tau}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(\tau), \mathbf{c})}\big[||f(\tau)\mathbf{Y}(\tau) - f(\tau_k)\mathbf{Y}(\tau_k)||^2\big]\mathrm{d}\tau\bigg] \\ &\lesssim \sum_{k=1}^{K} \int_{\tau_{k - 1}}^{\tau_k} \bigg[d(\Delta\tau)(\tau + 1)^3 +(\Delta\tau)^2 (M_2 + d)(\tau + 1)^4\bigg]\mathrm{d}\tau \\ &\lesssim \Delta\tau(M_2 + d)\int_{0}^{T_g}(\tau + 1)^4\mathrm{d} \tau\\ &\lesssim \Delta\tau(M_2 + d)(T_g + 1)^5, \end{align*} which completes the proof.

nodes.statement: Define an index threshold: \begin{align} k_1 := \min\{0\le k \le K: \tau_k \ge \min\{1, T_g/2\}\}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement_short: Split diffusion times at a Lipschitz threshold: Lemma 7 for small times and Lemma 8 (stochastic localization) for large times, then sum.
nodes.statement:
From \eqref{eq: forward_SDE_coeff}, we note that $\lambda_	au\sigma_	au^{-2}$ is decreasing in $	au$, with $\lim_{	au 	o 0+}\lambda_	au\sigma_	au^{-2} = +\infty$ and $\lim_{	au 	o \infty}\lambda_	au\sigma_	au^{-2} = 0$. Hence, for the given condition $\mathbf{c}$, there must exist $	au_0$ such that $\lambda_{	au_0}\sigma_{	au_0}^{-2} = 2L(\mathbf{c})$. This allows us to apply Lemma ef{lemma: lipschitz_score_diff_bound} for $	au < \min\{	au_0, 	au_{k_1}\}$. However, when $L(\mathbf{c})$ is small, $	au_0$ can be large. To control the magnitude of (the sum of) $(	au_k + 1)^6$ in Lemma ef{lemma: lipschitz_score_diff_bound}, we introduce a larger Lipschitz constant  egin{align} L_2(\mathbf{c}) := L(\mathbf{c}) + \lambda_{\min\{1,T_g/2\}}\sigma_{\min\{1, T_g/2\}}^{-2}. \end{align} It is clear that $
abla\log q_0(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$ is also $L_2(\mathbf{c})$-Lipschitz continuous. We can then define  egin{align*} 	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c}) = \max ig\{0\le 	au\le T_g: \lambda_	au\sigma_	au^{-2} \ge 2L_2(\mathbf{c}) ig\}. \end{align*} Note that $\lambda_{\min\{1, T_g/2\}}\sigma_{\min\{1, T_g/2\}}^{-2} \le 2L_2(\mathbf{c})$ and $\lambda_	au\sigma_	au^{-2}$ is decreasing in $	au$. Thus, for any given and fixed condition $\mathbf{c}$, $	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c}) < \min\{1, T_g/2\} \le 	au_{k_1}.$ Let $k_{0}(\mathbf{c}) = \min\{1\le k \le K: 	au_k \ge 	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c})\}\le k_1$. We can now apply Lemma ef{lemma: lipschitz_score_diff_bound} with settings of $s = 	au_1, \cdots, 	au_{k_{0}(\mathbf{c}) - 1}$ and $s = 	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c})$. Then, for $\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_{	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{c}),\mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k | 	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{c})$,  egin{align*} & \sum_{k=1}^{k_{0}(\mathbf{c}) - 1}\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_{k}}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k))}  ig[\|g^2(	au)
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c})\|^2 ig]\mathrm{d} 	au \ & \qquad + \int_{	au_{k_{0}(\mathbf{c}) - 1}}^{	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c})}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{Y}(	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}))}  ig[\|g^2(	au)
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})})
abla\log q_{	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}) | \mathbf{c})\|^2 ig]\mathrm{d} 	au\ &\lesssim d(\Delta	au)^2L_2(\mathbf{c})(L_2(\mathbf{c}) + 1) igg[\sum_{k=1}^{k_0(\mathbf{c})} (	au_k + 1)^6 igg]\ &\lesssim d(\Delta	au)^2L_2(\mathbf{c})(L_2(\mathbf{c}) + 1)k_0(\mathbf{c}), \end{align*} where we use the fact that $	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}\le 	au_{k_1} \le 1 + \Delta	au$. Note that when $	au = 	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c})\le 1$, we can apply \eqref{eq: expoenetial_approximation} to obtain  egin{align*} 2L_2(\mathbf{c}) \asymp  rac{\lambda_	au}{\sigma_	au^2} =  rac{e^{- rac{a}{4}	au^2 -  rac{b}{2}	au}}{1 - e^{- rac{a}{2}	au^2 - b	au}} \asymp  rac{1 - a	au^2/4 - b	au /2}{a	au^2/2 + b	au} =  rac{1}{a	au^2/2 + b	au} -  rac{1}{2} \asymp  rac{1}{	au} -  rac{1}{2}, \end{align*} yielding  egin{align} 	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c}) \asymp  rac{2}{4L_2(\mathbf{c}) + 1},\quad k_0(\mathbf{c}) \asymp  rac{2}{(4L_2(\mathbf{c}) + 1)\Delta	au}. \end{align} Therefore,  egin{align} & \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[\sum_{k=1}^{k_{0}(\mathbf{c}) - 1}\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_{k}}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k))}  ig[\|g^2(	au)
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c})\|^2 ig]\mathrm{d} 	au igg] 
onumber\ & \quad + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[\int_{	au_{k_{0}(\mathbf{c}) - 1}}^{	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c})}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{Y}(	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}))}  ig[\|g^2(	au)
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})})
abla\log q_{	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}) | \mathbf{c})\|^2 ig]\mathrm{d} 	au igg] 
onumber\ &\lesssim \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} ig[d(\Delta	au)^2L_2(\mathbf{c})(L_2(\mathbf{c}) + 1)k_0(\mathbf{c}) ig] 
onumber\ &\overset{\eqref{eq: lipz_index_approximation}}{\lesssim} d\Delta	au\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} ig[L_2(\mathbf{c}) + 1 ig]
onumber\ &= d\Delta	au\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} ig[L(\mathbf{c}) + \lambda_{\min\{1, T_g/2\}}\sigma_{\min\{1, T_g/2\}}^{-2} + 1 ig] 
onumber\ &\lesssim d\Delta	au(L_1 + 1), \end{align} where $L_1$ is defined in \eqref{eq: convergence_lipschitz}, and the last step follows from the approximation that  egin{align} \lambda_{\min\{1, T_g/2\}}\sigma_{\min\{1, T_g/2\}}^{-2} \asymp  rac{1}{a(\min\{1, T_g/2\})^2/2 + b\min\{1, T_g/2\}} -  rac{1}{2} \asymp 1. \end{align} On the other hand, for those $k \ge k_0(\mathbf{c})$, Lemma ef{lemma: score_diff_bound_large_t} implies that  egin{align} & \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[\int_{	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c})}^{	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}} \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{Y}(	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}))} ig[\|g^2(	au)
abla\log q_{	au}(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})})
abla\log q_{	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_{k_0(\mathbf{c})}) | \mathbf{c} ) \|^2 ig] \mathrm{d}	au igg]
onumber\ & \quad + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[\sum_{k=k_0(\mathbf{c}) + 1}^{K }\int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{	au_k}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k))} ig[\|g^2(	au)
abla\log q_{	au}(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c} ) \|^2 ig] \mathrm{d}	au igg]
onumber\ &\lesssim \Delta	au (T_g + 1)^2 \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}}  ig[\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(0)\sim p_{	ext{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}  ig[\|\mathbf{Y}(0)\|^2 ig] ig] + d\Delta	au\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[\ln igg( rac{1}{	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c})}  igg) +  rac{1}{	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c})} + (T_g + 1)^4  igg] 
onumber\ &\overset{\eqref{eq: lipz_index_approximation}}{\lesssim} M_2\Delta	au (T_g + 1)^2 + d\Delta	au \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} ig[\ln(2L_2(\mathbf{c}) + 1/2) + 2L_2(\mathbf{c}) + 1/2 + (T_g + 1)^4  ig] 
onumber\ &\lesssim M_2\Delta	au (T_g + 1)^2 + d\Delta	au  ig[L_1 + (T_g + 1)^4  ig], \end{align} where in the last step we use the fact that $\ln(x + 1/2) \le x + 1/2$ for any $x\ge 0$ and the approximation in \eqref{eq: threshold_approximation}. The proof is complete by combining \eqref{eq: score_error_bound_1} and \eqref{eq: score_error_bound_2}.

onumber\ &\lesssim \Delta	au (T_g + 1)^2 \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}}  ig[\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(0)\sim p_{	ext{target}}(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}  ig[\|\mathbf{Y}(0)\|^2 ig] ig] + d\Delta	au\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{c}\sim\mathbf{C}} igg[\ln igg( rac{1}{	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c})}  igg) +  rac{1}{	au_{lipz}(\mathbf{c})} + (T_g + 1)^4  igg]

abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)

onumber\ &\qquad + 2\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k))} ig[g^4(	au_k)\|
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - 
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c})\|^2 ig]
onumber\ &\overset{	ext{(i)}}{\le} 2 ig[ ig(g^2(	au) - g^2(	au_k) ig)^2 + 2g^4(	au_k) ig(\lambda_{	au, 	au_k}^{-1} - 1 ig)^2 ig] \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)} ig[\|
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c})\|^2]
onumber\ &\qquad + 8\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k))} ig[g^4(	au_k)\|
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - 
abla\log q_{	au}(\lambda_{	au, 	au_k}^{-1}\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c})\|^2 ig]
onumber\ &\overset{	ext{(ii)}}{\lesssim} (	au_k - 	au)^2(	au_k + 1)^4 \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)} ig[\|
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c})\|^2]
onumber\ &\qquad + (	au_k + 1)^2\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k))} ig[\|
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - 
abla\log q_{	au}(\lambda_{	au, 	au_k}^{-1}\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c})\|^2 ig] \end{align} where the inequality (i) is from Lemma 11 of \cite{chen2023improved}, and the inequality (ii) employs the approximation that for small $	au_k - 	au$,  egin{align*} \lambda^{-1}_{	au, 	au_k} - 1 = e^{ rac{a}{4}(	au_k^2 - 	au^2) +  rac{b}{2}(	au_k - 	au)} - 1\lesssim  rac{a}{4}(	au_k^2 - 	au^2) +  rac{b}{2}(	au_k - 	au) \lesssim (	au_k - 	au)(	au_k + 1). \end{align*} Next, from the condition that $\sigma_{s}^2\le  rac{\lambda_{s}}{2L(\mathbf{c})}$ and the fact that $\lambda_	au\sigma_	au^{-2}$ is decreasing in $	au$, we know that $\sigma_{	au}^2\le  rac{\lambda_{	au}}{2L(\mathbf{c})}$ for all $	au \le s$, indicating that Lemma 14 of \cite{chen2023improved} holds and $
abla\log q_	au(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$ is $(2L(\mathbf{c})\lambda_	au^{-1})$-Lipschitz on $\mathbb{R}^d$ for all $	au \le s$. Then,  egin{align*} &\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_	au(\cdot | \mathbf{c}), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k | 	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{c})}[\|
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - 
abla\log q_{	au}(\lambda_{	au, 	au_k}^{-1}\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c})\|^2] \ &\le 4L^2(\mathbf{c})\lambda_	au^{-2}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k))}  ig[\|\mathbf{Y}(	au) - \lambda_{	au, 	au_k}^{-1} \mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\|^2 ig]\ &= 4dL^2(\mathbf{c})\lambda_	au^{-2} \lambda_{	au,	au_k}^{-2} \sigma^2_{	au, 	au_k} = 4d L^2(\mathbf{c})e^{ rac{a}{2}	au_k^2 + b	au_k} ig[1 - e^{- rac{a}{2}(	au_k^2 - 	au^2) - b(	au_k - 	au)} ig]\ &\overset{\eqref{eq: expoenetial_approximation}}{\lesssim} d L^2(\mathbf{c})(1 + a	au_k^2/2 + b	au_k)\cdot(	au_k - 	au)(a	au_k + b) \ &\lesssim d L^2(\mathbf{c})(	au_k - 	au)(	au_k + 1)^3, \end{align*} where we use the condition that $k \le k_1$ so that we can apply \eqref{eq: expoenetial_approximation} to approximate $(\lambda_	au \lambda_{	au,	au_k})^{-2}$. Next, the Lipschitz continuity of $
abla\log q_	au(\cdot | \mathbf{c})$ implies that $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_	au(\cdot | \mathbf{c})}||
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c})\|^2 \le 2dL(\mathbf{c})\lambda_	au^{-1}$ as in Lemma 21 of \cite{chen2023improved}. Hence, we can infer from \eqref{eq: score_error_target} that  egin{align*} & \int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{s}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Y}(	au)\sim q_	au(\cdot | \mathbf{c}), \mathbf{Y}(	au_k)\sim q_{	au_k | 	au}(\cdot | \mathbf{Y}(	au), \mathbf{c})} ig[\|g^2(	au)
abla\log q_	au(\mathbf{Y}(	au) | \mathbf{c}) - g^2(	au_k)
abla\log q_{	au_k}(\mathbf{Y}(	au_k) | \mathbf{c})\|^2 ig]\mathrm{d} 	au \ &\lesssim \int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{s}(	au_k - 	au)^2(	au_k + 1)^4 dL(\mathbf{c})\lambda_	au^{-1} + d L^2(\mathbf{c})(	au_k - 	au)(	au_k + 1)^5 \mathrm{d} 	au\ &\lesssim \int_{	au_{k - 1}}^{s}(	au_k - 	au)^2(	au_k + 1)^6 dL(\mathbf{c}) + d L^2(\mathbf{c})(	au_k - 	au)(	au_k + 1)^5 \mathrm{d} 	au\ &\lesssim d(\Delta	au)^2L(\mathbf{c})(L(\mathbf{c}) + 1)(	au_k + 1)^6, \end{align*} where the second inequality is obtained by applying \eqref{eq: expoenetial_approximation} to approximate $\lambda_	au^{-1}$. The proof is complete.
